cues.text: The genotype features are used to train
the models while the metadata are used
only for auditing. We tested the auditor
on three tasks using data from the NCBI.
Eoline cyprofluxin, E.oli, Sephrioxone,
and Salmonella with cyprloxicin. For
each task, we trained rule-based
logistic regression and random forest
models. Under standard random train test
splits, performance was strong. Logistic
regression achieved F1 scores of 0.93
across the three tasks. This shows that
AMR genotype features contain strong
predictive signal. However, the
surveillance aware audits revealed a bit
more of a nuanced picture. The auditor
tested performance using S&P cluster
aware splits, country and location
holdouts, source holdouts, and isolation
type holdouts. These tests show that
high random split performance did not
necessarily always translate into stable
performances across these contexts. The
main weaknesses differ by task. E.coli
with cyproloxisin was most sensitive to
isolation type hold out. E.coli with
septrixone was sensitive to country and
isolation type hold out and salmonella
with cyprloxxyin showed the largest
instability over S&P cluster aware and
country held out evaluation.
We also found out that a could remain
high even when F1 dropped. This means
the model could still rank isolates
reasonably well, but its classification
threshold did not always transfer across
different surveillance settings.
Overall, our product shows that AMR
prediction models should not only be
evaluated with random test train splits,
and that our auditor provides a
reproducible workflow for reporting
model performance, subgroup reliability,
metadata completeness, and warning
flags. In conclusion, across three AMR
prediction tasks, random split
performance was consistently high, but
surveillance aware auditing revealed
task specific weaknesses that aggregate
metrics alone would have missed. Thank
you.
